explanations.explanation: Weep is right. Dibon goes up to its temple to weep at its high places. Ar and Kir were destroyed in a night, so nobody is heading up there for a party. I think this is a town taking its sorrow straight to its temple.

Dance would make a very different verse. The text says Dibon goes up to weep at its high places. Ar and Kir were destroyed in a night, and weeping is the word the verse gives. I run a bakery, not a dance floor, and even I'd sit this one out.
Singing is a nice thought, friend, but the verse says weep. Dibon goes up to its temple to weep at its high places. Moab wails over Nebo and Medeba too. Weeping is the word the verse uses.
True. The verse says “on the rooftops and in the public squares they all wail, falling down weeping.” In its streets they wear sackcloth too. The rooftops and the public squares are both named.

This one is true, friend. The verse says “on the rooftops and in the public squares they all wail, falling down weeping.” They wear sackcloth in its streets as well. The rooftops and the public squares are both named.
Not this time. The text says “…the soldiers of Moab cry out; their souls tremble within.” These are the fighting men, and they're trembling inside. Calm and steady isn't how the verse describes them.

False is right. The text says “…the soldiers of Moab cry out; their souls tremble within.” Even the men trained to hold the line are crying out. When the soldiers are shaking, you know how heavy the moment is.

It cries out, just as the verse says: “My heart cries out over Moab…” This is a burden against Moab, and still the speaker's heart is breaking as the ruin comes into view. I think that tells us how to listen to this prophecy. It's sorrowful, not smug.

Rejoicing isn't in the verse. It says “My heart cries out over Moab…” The speaker is looking at fugitives running and towns in ruins, and the heart answers with crying. I think that makes this a sad passage to read, not a happy one.

A hard heart is a good guess for a burden, but the verse says otherwise: “My heart cries out over Moab…” Nothing in the speaker's reaction is cold or stony. The fugitives flee, and the speaker's heart cries right along with them.

Their wealth and belongings, yes. The text says they carry them over the Brook of the Willows. Just before this, the grass is withered and the vegetation is gone. I think a person grabs what they can carry when the ground itself runs dry.

The soldiers do cry out in this passage, but the text never says they're carried anywhere. What it says is that the people carry their wealth and belongings over the Brook of the Willows. That's the only load named. Stick with what the verse puts in their hands.

No weapons or shields come up in this verse. The text says they carry their wealth and belongings over the Brook of the Willows. These people are fugitives, hauling what they own. It's more of a moving day than a march to battle.
True. Their outcry echoes to the border of Moab. The wailing reaches Eglaim and is heard in Beer-elim. That's wailing you can hear from place to place, and my oven timer can't do that.

This one is true, baker. The text says their outcry echoes to the border of Moab. Their wailing reaches Eglaim, and it is heard in Beer-elim. The sound doesn't stop in one town. It rolls right across the land.

A lion. The text says “…a lion upon the fugitives of Moab and upon the remnant of the land.” The waters of Dimon are already full of blood, and more is coming. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's worth slowing down for.

A flood is a fair guess with all those waters around. But the verse names a lion: “…a lion upon the fugitives of Moab and upon the remnant of the land.” The waters of Dimon are full of blood, and a lion is what's coming next. It's a heavy verse.

Locusts never show up in this passage. The text says “…a lion upon the fugitives of Moab and upon the remnant of the land.” The fugitives and the remnant are the ones in view. It's one of the heavy parts of this prophecy.

The mount of Daughter Zion. The command says to send the tribute lambs from Sela in the desert to the mount of Daughter Zion. They're sent to the ruler of the land, and the verse names that mountain as where they go. Sela in the desert is where they start.

Dibon's temple is where the people went to weep, back in chapter 15. The lambs in this verse go somewhere else. The command says to send them from Sela in the desert to the mount of Daughter Zion. The ruler of the land is who they're meant for.

Babylon isn't named anywhere in this passage. The command says to send the tribute lambs from Sela in the desert to the mount of Daughter Zion. That's the whole route. No palace is on the map for this one.

Shelter is right. The plea says “Shelter us at noonday with shade as dark as night. Hide the refugees; do not betray the one who flees.” They're asking for a place to hide, not a place to fight. I think that's how desperate people ask when they're running.

Weapons aren't in this plea. What it asks for is shelter: “Hide the refugees; do not betray the one who flees.” It asks for counsel and a decision too. It asks for a place to stay, not something to swing.

Revenge isn't in the plea. It asks for counsel and a decision, and for shelter: “Let my fugitives stay with you; be a refuge for Moab from the destroyer.” The destroyer is who the refuge is from. Revenge never comes up.

David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3). The text says a throne will be established in the tent of David, in loving devotion. That comes after the oppressor has gone and destruction has ceased. It's a bright spot in a dark chapter.

Saul was Israel's first king (1 Samuel 10:1), but the verse doesn't name him. It says a throne will be established in the tent of David. Remember, this follows the oppressor going away and destruction ceasing. David is the name on this tent.

Moab is all over this passage, so I get why it caught your eye. But the verse says a throne will be established in the tent of David, in loving devotion. That's after the oppressor has gone and destruction has ceased. Moab's name is everywhere else, but this tent has David's name on it.
Not quite, friend. The text says this judge is “…seeking justice and hastening righteousness…” He sits on the throne in faithfulness. Quick to do right is the opposite of what the card says.
False is right. The text says the judge is “…seeking justice and hastening righteousness…” He sits on the throne in faithfulness. He hurries toward what is right, not away from it.

Empty is right. The verse says “But his boasting is empty.” All that pomposity, pride and overflowing arrogance, and the boasting has nothing behind it. It's a big voice with nothing inside, like a fancy cookie box with no cookies.

Earned would make the boasting solid, but the verse says the opposite. It says “But his boasting is empty.” Moab's pride and conceit are loud, and nothing backs them up. The noise is bigger than the substance.
Ancient isn't what the verse says. It says “But his boasting is empty.” The talk about Moab's pride is all about how big it is, not how old. Big words, nothing behind them.

explanations.answer: The fields and vines are ruined
explanations.explanation: The fields and vines are ruined. The verse gives the reason: “For the fields of Heshbon have withered, along with the grapevines of Sibmah.” The rulers of the nations have also trampled the choicest vines. I think the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth are a taste of what's been lost.

Traders aren't mentioned here. The reason the verse gives is that the fields of Heshbon have withered, along with the grapevines of Sibmah. The rulers of the nations have trampled the choicest vines too. The problem is the land itself.

No robbery shows up in this passage. The verse says “…the fields of Heshbon have withered, along with the grapevines of Sibmah.” The rulers of the nations have trampled the choicest vines. The loss is in the fields and the vines.

Weeps with Jazer, just like the verse says: “So I weep with Jazer for the vines of Sibmah…” The speaker also drenches Heshbon and Elealeh with tears. I think that's someone who isn't standing at a distance, crying right alongside Jazer.
Mocking isn't in this verse. It says “So I weep with Jazer for the vines of Sibmah…” The speaker drenches Heshbon and Elealeh with tears, too. Tears are what the speaker brings, not jokes.
Nobody plants anything in this verse. It says “So I weep with Jazer for the vines of Sibmah…” The vines are trampled and the speaker's response is tears. Replanting isn't in the picture.
True. The verse says “Therefore my heart laments for Moab like a harp, my inmost being for Kir-heres.” The lament reaches the speaker's inmost being. I think it sounds like a harp playing a sad song.

This one is true, friend. The verse says “Therefore my heart laments for Moab like a harp, my inmost being for Kir-heres.” The lament reaches the speaker's inmost being. That's sorrow deep inside, not just on the surface.

Not here. The verse says that when Moab wearies himself and enters his sanctuary to pray, “…it will do him no good.” He can wear himself out all he wants and it won't turn things around. All that effort, and the verse says it doesn't help.

False is right. The verse says that when Moab appears on the high place, wearies himself and enters his sanctuary to pray, “…it will do him no good.” Wearing himself out doesn't change that. The verse says it plainly.

An object of contempt. The LORD says “In three years, as a hired worker counts the years, Moab’s splendor will become an object of contempt, with all her many people.” A hired worker counts the years carefully, and this is the count. The splendor won't stay splendid.

A wonder to the nations sounds grand, but the LORD says something else. He says “In three years, as a hired worker counts the years, Moab’s splendor will become an object of contempt, with all her many people.” The splendor becomes contempt, not a wonder.

A crown for Zion isn't what the LORD says. He says “In three years, as a hired worker counts the years, Moab’s splendor will become an object of contempt, with all her many people.” The word for what the splendor becomes is contempt.

No, friend, it's the other way around. The LORD says “And those who are left will be few and feeble.” Few is the opposite of many, and feeble is the opposite of strong. The people who remain won't number much or have much strength.
False is right. The LORD says “And those who are left will be few and feeble.” That's the opposite of many and strong. It's a sober ending to a heavy passage.
